title: Fractions on the Number Line: Distance and Intermediate Numbers

blocks.text: A number line requires the same origin and the same unit when comparing its points. The unit is the segment from zero to one; it can contain many marks. Negative numbers appear to the left of zero. Counting intervals rather than tick marks lets you read a point even when its label is hidden.

blocks.prompt: The distance from −1 to 0 represents one unit divided into fourths. The indicated point lies exactly halfway between two neighboring marks. Write its position as a fraction in simplest form with a positive denominator.

feedback.correct: Each half of a one-fourth interval equals one eighth. The point is eleven eighths to the left of zero: −11/8 = −1−3/8.
feedback.incorrect: The point does not coincide with a quarter mark: it lies halfway through an interval. Refine fourths into eighths and preserve the negative direction.

blocks.prompt: A point is at −7/6. Write its distance from zero and how far it must move to the right to reach 1/3.

feedback.correct: The distance from zero is 7/6. The movement is 1/3−(−7/6) = 3/2: it crosses zero and continues one third.
feedback.incorrect: The position has a sign; a distance is not negative. Subtracting −7/6 requires adding its opposite to measure the movement.

blocks.text: The difference between two positions measures a directed displacement. To find the distance between points, take the positive difference between the greater and lesser values. This gives subtraction with signed numbers a geometric interpretation.

blocks.prompt: Two marks are at 5/8 and 11/12. What is the distance between them?

feedback.correct: 11/12 = 22/24 and 5/8 = 15/24. The distance is 7/24 of a unit.
feedback.incorrect: Adding the positions measures a different relationship. Find the distance by subtracting the smaller position from the larger one.

blocks.text: There Are Other Fractions Between Two Fractions

Between 1/3 and 2/3 lies 1/2. We can see this in sixths: 2/6 < 3/6 < 4/6. If two fractions seem consecutive within a partition, refine that partition. Between 1/5 and 2/5 lies 3/10, because 2/10 < 3/10 < 4/10. There is no immediate "next rational number."

blocks.prompt: 7/12 and 2/3 can be written as 14/24 and 16/24. Construct the fraction exactly halfway between them; use denominator 24.

feedback.correct: 15/24 is one twenty-fourth away from each endpoint. It can be simplified to 5/8, but here the fields show the construction in twenty-fourths.
feedback.incorrect: 14/24 and 16/24 are endpoints, not interior points. The finer partition leaves an integer numerator between fourteen and sixteen.

blocks.prompt: Using denominator 16, construct a fraction strictly between −3/4 and −5/8.

feedback.correct: −3/4 = −12/16 and −5/8 = −10/16; between them lies −11/16. It is the only intermediate integer numerator with that denominator.
feedback.incorrect: −13/16 would lie to the left of both endpoints; −9/16 would lie to their right. With negative fractions, numerator order is still preserved when the denominator is the same and positive.

blocks.text: A general construction is to take the midpoint. If a < b, the distance b−a is positive. Starting at a, move half that distance: a+(b−a)/2 = (a+b)/2. You move some distance, but less than the full distance, so the new number lies between the two. If a and b are rational, these operations produce another rational number.

feedback.correct: Their sum is −3/10 and half of it is −3/20. That lies between −8/20 and 2/20.
feedback.incorrect: The sum alone is not the midpoint: you must also divide by two. The sign of the midpoint depends on where the endpoints lie.

blocks.prompt: Someone claims that 1/100 and 2/100 are consecutive rational numbers. Which counterexample disproves this claim?

options.label: 3/200, because 2/200 < 3/200 < 4/200.
options.reviewFeedback: Check that the proposed number satisfies both strict comparisons and that the new partition preserves the original endpoints.

options.label: 3/100, because three is greater than two.
options.reviewFeedback: Your explanation shows that one numerator is greater than another. To disprove the claim that the numbers are consecutive, also check where the proposed point must lie relative to both endpoints.

options.label: 0, because every interval contains zero.
options.reviewFeedback: Your reasoning claims that every interval contains zero. Place zero and the proposed interval's endpoints on a number line to examine that generalization.

feedback.correct: Refining hundredths into two-hundredths produces an interior point: 3/200. The partition can be refined again and again.
feedback.incorrect: 3/100 is outside the interval, and so is zero. A counterexample must satisfy both inequalities.

blocks.prompt: Select all numbers strictly between −1/2 and 1/4.

options.reviewFeedback: For the selected negative fraction, compare its position with both bounds. Distinguish distance from the origin from order on the number line.
For the selected fraction, review the condition "strictly" when comparing it with each endpoint.
For the selected positive fraction, check both bounds using equal-sized parts. The sign alone does not determine whether it belongs to the interval.
For the selected fraction in thirds, check its exact relationship with the upper bound and keep the comparison with the lower bound as well.
For the selected zero, locate the origin relative to the two bounds. Check both inequalities without assuming that every interval contains zero.

feedback.correct: −3/8, 0, and 1/8 lie inside. −1/2 is an excluded endpoint, and 1/3 exceeds 1/4.
feedback.incorrect: The word "between" requires two comparisons. The sign alone does not tell you whether a number is in the interval.

blocks.prompt: The same length measures 3/4 of a unit A. A unit B is twice as long as A. How long is the length when measured in units B?

options.label: 3/2 of B.
options.reviewFeedback: Check the physical length represented by your chosen measurement when you use the new unit. Changing units must preserve the original length.

options.label: 3/4 of B.
options.reviewFeedback: Your choice keeps the numerical measurement unchanged. Check whether that number can stay the same when the size of the unit changes.

options.label: 3/8 of B.
options.reviewFeedback: Check your measurement by reconstructing the length using the new unit's size. The physical quantity must remain unchanged during conversion.

feedback.correct: Since A equals half of B, three quarters of A equal three eighths of B. A larger unit gives a smaller numerical measurement for the same length.
feedback.incorrect: 3/2 would double the physical quantity. Keeping 3/4 overlooks the change of unit, even though the length stayed the same.
